column3: It depicts the Day's hushed submission before the Most Merciful, supplying the focus's court setting.
It establishes an appointed Day of decisive separation for all, supporting the focus's judicial Day.
Forgiveness after a legal warning helps hold mercy and accountable judgment together.
It nearly restates the focus: dominion belongs to God that Day and He judges between people.
The preceding opened-sky and angelic descent scene directly introduces the Day named in the focus.
It identifies God as the Real and contrasts truth with deviation, clarifying the focus's "the true."
Disbelievers themselves call it a difficult Day, directly paralleling the focus's final clause.
The local catalogue of destroyed generations only broadly reinforces the surah's warning context.
It foregrounds the Most Merciful and Merciful names that qualify the focus's sovereign.
Its concise description of that Day as difficult confirms the same eschatological severity after 54:8.
Present blindness becoming greater path-loss in the Hereafter offers a limited account of unbelievers' plight.
Creation in truth and the return to God gives a broad backdrop to rightful dominion.
On that Day God gives the full due in truth and makes His manifest reality known, closely expanding the focus.
The same surah's Day brings no good news to criminals, a direct antecedent to its hardship for disbelievers.
God's ownership of heavens and earth gives the focus's Day-specific dominion its universal scope.
Fear of a Day whose evil spreads outward reinforces the focus's description of a hard Day.
The destruction of powerful criminal generations offers only a general precedent for the disbelievers' hardship.
God grants and removes dominion, explaining why all rule in the focus belongs to Him rather than human claimants.
The false attribution of a child to the Most Merciful marks a challenge to the unique divine authority named in the focus.
The wrongdoer's regret immediately after the focus continues the surah's portrayal of that Day's distress.
Ease alongside hardship is a limited contrast to the irreversible hardship assigned to disbelievers on that Day.
It joins truth, divine dominion, and a trumpet Day, strongly illuminating the focus's combined terms.
Thrown fragments of hearing and lying do not clarify the focus's sovereign Day.
A plea for mercy gives a distant devotional use of mercy, not the focus's judicial setting.
Its rejection of a child for the Most Merciful only indirectly protects the divine uniqueness in the focus.
Being led from remembrance is a local cause of path-loss, with only indirect bearing on the Day's hardship.
It repeats the preceding ease-with-hardship statement without adding to the focus.
Iblis's arrogant unbelief supplies a general model of defiance, not the focus's judgment scene.
Pharaoh's public claim to dominion forms a useful contrast with the rightful dominion of the focus.
It rejects rival gods when the Most Merciful wills harm, only broadly supporting sole divine authority.
Public disgrace and evil for disbelievers on Resurrection Day helps specify the focus's hardship.
The local image of people gathered face-down to Hell extends the surah's grim Day-of-judgment outcome.
The isolated name Most Merciful keeps the focus's mercy-qualified sovereignty in view, though earlier evidence is fuller.
It rejects a child for the Most Merciful, a limited reinforcement of His unshared status.
Repeated praise in Moses's mission does not clarify the sovereign Day.
It calls that Day the true Day and directs people to their Lord, directly reinforcing the focus's declaration.
Fear of a grim, severe Day supplies another perspective on the Day's difficulty.
The local denial of resurrection supplies a remote cause for the Day's punishment.
Truth from the Lord and fire promised to its rejecters connect divine truth with the disbelievers' outcome.
It names God the true King, a close theological parallel to the focus's true dominion.
Repeated remembrance in Moses's mission does not clarify the focus's sovereign Day.
The people's demand in the Lot narrative has no clear bearing on the focus.
Satan's disobedience to the Most Merciful gives only a general pattern of rebellion.
The local destruction of people who denied signs reinforces the surah's warning framework.
All creation praises God and His is dominion, a broad but relevant support for the focus.
Woe for deniers on that Day directly supports the difficult consequence for disbelievers.
Divine sight over Moses and Aaron does not clarify the focus.
Making a people kings is a historical grant of status, only distantly related to divine dominion.
The estimate of time spent does not add to the focus's meaning.
The local drowning of Noah's deniers and prepared painful punishment extends the surah's judgment pattern.
The demand for an angel and immediate decision offers only a limited warning parallel.
God is named the true King, though the surrounding request for knowledge makes it less direct than 23:116.
The Messenger's complaint that his people abandoned the Quran helps explain the local rejection under judgment.
Noah's appeal to the truthful, wisest Judge is a distant parallel to rightful divine rule.
Iblis's refusal and unbelief provide a broad antecedent of defiance.
Followers blame leaders for leading them from the path, supplying a cause of punished misguidance.
The creation announcement to angels does not clarify the focus.
It asks how unbelievers can guard against a Day that turns children gray, intensifying the focus's hardship.
The immediate local warning that wrongdoers will taste great punishment directly supports the focus's severity.
Rejecting truth and later receiving its news gives a general pattern behind the focus's outcome.
Dominion is in God's hand and He has power over everything, broadly grounding the focus's claim.
God's deity in heaven and earth and final return only indirectly bears on the Day's dominion.
Being eased toward hardship concerns a moral path rather than the focus's final Day.
The everlasting path of Hell gives a concrete dimension to the hard fate of disbelievers.
God answers objections with truth and best explanation, contributing to the local truth-versus-rejection setting.
The marriage prohibitions do not clarify the focus.
Noah's call to his unbelieving son is only a remote narrative parallel to rejecting salvation.
Obstinacy toward divine signs gives a general cause for the difficult Day.
The divine word becoming binding on disbelievers as people of the Fire strongly supports the focus's just severity.
Making truth prevail and cutting off disbelievers in battle is not the focus's final court.
The local preparation of blazing fire for those who deny the Hour is a direct premise for the focus.
Repentance and forgiveness offer a limited alternative to the hard outcome.
Each person earning sin against himself only broadly supports individual accountability.
Merciful delay before an inescapable appointment distinctly relates mercy to eventual judgment in the focus.
Humiliating punishment for those who fabricate against God and reject His signs parallels the disbelievers' outcome.
Mercy toward believers in an hour of hardship forms a limited contrast with hardship for disbelievers.
Proportionate burden, forgiveness, and mercy add a distinct account of accountable yet merciful divine dealing.
Angelic forgiveness and divine mercy are not closely tied to the focus's sovereign Day.
The revival sign and personal certainty do not clarify the focus's judgment claim.
Revelation as guidance and mercy for believers only broadly contrasts reception of the focus's truth.
The Day's concealment ends and God alone is proclaimed sovereign, closely paralleling and sharpening the focus.
Order in the Most Merciful's creation gives only a distant image of His merciful rule.
The true balance on that Day supplies the judicial measure implicit in the focus's rightful dominion.
The religion of truth prevailing over resistance is not the focus's eschatological scene.
The God-fearing are gathered to the Most Merciful as honored delegates, a strong counterpoint to disbelievers' hardship.
Its assertion of certain truth reinforces the focus's true reality, though without its Day or dominion.
No soul controls anything for another on that Day and command belongs to God, directly supporting sole dominion.
God's enmity toward disbelievers gives only a general punitive relation.
Turning punishment away on that Day is called mercy, directly clarifying mercy alongside the focus's hardship.
The procedure for disputed testimony does not illuminate the focus.
Hell displayed to disbelievers on that Day gives a concrete scene for their hardship.
One God named Most Merciful and Merciful only broadly supports the focus's divine title.
Creation in truth and recompense for every soul without injustice directly explain rightful final judgment.
Turning away from each new reminder of the Most Merciful helps account for the disbelievers' eventual hardship.
The ranks of charitable fighters and inheritance of creation do not clarify the focus.
The Quran is mercy for believers yet increases wrongdoers in loss, supplying a distinct reception-based contrast.
The household and meal permissions have no relation to the focus.
The Lord and angels arriving in ranks provides a limited formal-court image.
Concealing guidance brings divine curse, only broadly related to rejecting truth.
The Lord's word becoming due upon persistent transgressors supports the justice of the hard outcome.
God's mastery of the Day of Judgment gives the clearest direct counterpart to the focus's rightful dominion on that Day.
All faces humble themselves before the Living, Self-Subsisting One, making the focus's sovereign court concrete.
The just scales set up for Resurrection Day explain how dominion on that Day is true and non-arbitrary.
The local demand to see angels is answered by the very Day when criminals see them without good news.
The nullification of deeds on that Day supplies a direct judicial consequence within the focus's immediate sequence.
The contrasting excellent abode and resting place for the people of Paradise sharpens the hardship of disbelievers.
The wrongdoer's regret over taking a companion continues the Day-of-distress scene immediately after the focus.
The divine statement that every prophet has an enemy helps frame the surah's resistant audience before judgment.
The disbelievers' objection to gradual revelation supplies a local form of resistance behind the focus's warning.
The fate of Moses's deniers extends the surah's accumulated precedent of rejected messengers and judgment.
The parables and destruction of prior communities reinforce the local warning that precedes the focus.
God's grasp of earth and folded heavens on Resurrection Day gives overwhelming scale to the focus's dominion.
The trumpet blast and universal collapse introduce the decisive Day on which all sovereignty is disclosed.
The earth shining by its Lord, the record, prophets, and witnesses depicts the true court of the focus.
Those who disbelieved being driven to Hell gives a direct outcome for the focus's hard Day.
Angels surrounding the Throne and judgment in truth complete the focus's court-and-dominion imagery.
A warning of a painful Day for wrongdoers directly reinforces the focus's hardship for disbelievers.
God's is the dominion of heavens and earth, and the falsifiers lose when the Hour comes.
The trumpet comes with the true promise, bringing the Day of warning into effect.
Radiant faces looking toward their Lord offer a decisive positive counterpart to the focus's hardship for disbelievers.
Gloomy faces expecting a calamity provide the opposing Day-of-judgment condition.
None speaks except by the Most Merciful's permission on the Day, showing His unchallengeable authority.
Hell set ablaze supplies the punitive scene underlying the Day's hardship for disbelievers.
The repeated question about the Day of Recompense intensifies the focus's eschatological designation.
Its second question preserves the overwhelming gravity of that Day beyond ordinary estimation.
The prospect of being raised for a tremendous Day directly supports the focus's Day of final rule.
The sky's splitting in obedience to its Lord supplies an apocalyptic disclosure of divine authority.
The earth's obedience to its Lord matches the universal submission implied by rightful dominion.
The earth crushed and leveled introduces the final Day's irreversible public manifestation.
People scattered like moths on that Day give a vivid collective scene of powerless dependence.
